opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what stood out most was how much of the release came down to taking safety and evaluation work seriously as a core part of shipping, not something bolted on at the end. o1 was a different kind of model. It reasons before it answers, so a lot of our existing assumptions about how to measure capabilities and risks didn't quite carry over cleanly. We had to think hard about which evaluations actually captured what the model could do, and where it might surprise us.

It was also very collaborative. Research, safety, policy, and product were all in the room together, asking: what do we actually know about this model, what don't we know yet, and what do we need to be confident about before people start using it? That kind of cross-functional pressure-testing was really energizing.

And I think there's a broader lesson there. As models get more capable, the measurement problem gets harder and more important. Being able to say clearly "here's what this model can and can't do" becomes a big part of releasing something responsibly. For me, o1 made that feel very concrete.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what stood out most was how much the evaluation work had to change. Up until then, a lot of our evals were built around the assumption that the model answers right away. With o1, you suddenly had a model that would think for a while before answering, and that broke a lot of our assumptions about how to measure it.

So one big thing was realizing that test-time compute was now a real axis. The same model could look quite different depending on how long you let it reason, and we had to figure out how to report that honestly rather than just picking the best number.

The second thing was how many of our benchmarks saturated faster than we expected. Things like competition math and some of the science question sets went from being meaningful differentiators to being close to solved in a pretty short window. That pushed us to build harder evals, and to think more about tasks that look like actual work rather than exam questions.

And the third piece was safety. Because the model reasons before it answers, you get a window into its thought process, and that opened up new ways to look at things like whether the model was following its instructions or trying to game a task. It also raised harder questions about what we should and shouldn't surface to users. Those discussions were some of the most interesting parts of the release for me, because they weren't purely technical. They were about what responsible deployment of a reasoning model actually looks like.

So overall, it felt less like shipping another model and more like the first step into a new paradigm, where a lot of the tooling and the evaluation methodology had to be rebuilt alongside it.

astra-6.text: For me, what stands out is the question of how you know a model is ready to release. It’s not just whether it can do something impressive; it’s whether you understand where it works, where it still struggles, and how to communicate that to users. That’s the part of the o1 release process I’d want to unpack.
